summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level provisions targeting morality. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

Enforcement also takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveler in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy now frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing directly to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

North Sumatra stands within this framework as one of the provinces singled out by OutRight Action International's 2022 study Creeping Criminalisation, which maps Indonesian national laws and regional regulations that violate the human rights of women and LGBTIQ people. The study examined eight focus provinces, among them North Sumatra, and found much overlap between them but significant regional variation in dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear. The authors state that their findings remain valid for regions outside the focus set, so a visitor to North Sumatra should expect local rules of this kind even where they are not separately documented.

No local bylaw specifically targeting transgender people in North Sumatra, and no enforcement action against a trans person in the province, is documented in the sources reviewed. The one legal-process data point from the province concerns Dimas Cahya, a transgender man in the state capital who became the first trans man there to change his name legally to match his identity. The Medan District Court granted the application after a six-week process. The presiding judge warned that the change would 'erase my identity' but took no position on LGBTI matters, and the case records no enforcement action against the applicant.
tangentialFactors:
Regional variation is the central practical complication in North Sumatra. OutRight Action International found significant differences between the eight provinces it examined in how dress codes, curfews and appearance restrictions are applied to transgender people, and it warns that its findings hold beyond the provinces it studied. A rule enforceable against a trans person in one province may be absent or applied differently in the next, and the sources do not catalogue the specific bylaws in force in North Sumatra.

The neighbouring province of Aceh operates a separate religious legal order under which two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025, and its punishments apply to anyone within the provincial boundary, including foreign visitors. Travellers routing through or toward Aceh from North Sumatra leave the framework described here for one with documented corporal punishment.

The national picture is one of tightening rather than easing. Police raids on private gatherings have been documented at least since June 2025, and the October 2025 presidential decree places LGBTQ+ people inside the official doctrine of national defence policy, which commentators quoted by ABC News tie to a subsequent wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women.
localsOnly:
Dimas Cahya's case in the state capital is the only documented instance in the sources of a trans person from the province obtaining a legal name change. The Medan District Court granted the application after a six-week process, with the judge warning that the change would 'erase my identity' while declining to engage with LGBTI questions. No enforcement action against him or the couple is recorded.

Medan is described by UNAIDS as conservative, with LGBTI people there deemed 'immoral', and a Medan legal-aid organisation put invasive questions to Cahya and his partner before the case proceeded. Residents seeking comparable relief should expect a similar administrative and social environment, and should not assume that a granted application protects against subsequent mistreatment.

OutRight Action International's study names North Sumatra as one of eight focus provinces with regional regulations discriminatory toward women and LGBTIQ people, including provisions touching sexual orientation and gender expression. Residents are exposed to these provincial rules directly, and to the dress-code, curfew and appearance restrictions that the study found to vary by province.
outOfScopeNotes:
No specific North Sumatra bylaw text, its enforcement record, or any documented police action against a transgender person in the province is present in the sources reviewed. The provincial legal position is therefore evidenced only through OutRight Action International's finding that its focus provinces carry discriminatory regulations and through the absence of contrary documentation, not through a named and dated local statute.

It is unresolved whether the name-change relief obtained by Dimas Cahya in 2021 is available on the same terms to foreign visitors or to residents presenting different circumstances, and whether any marker or identity-document rule applies to travellers entering the province. No source in the inventory addresses document screening at Indonesian entry points.

The claim that reporting from August 2026 ties the October 2025 presidential decree to vigilante attacks on transgender women is carried from the parent framework without the underlying attack data, including whether any such incident occurred in North Sumatra specifically.
